accroche: To judge a rule just, imagine it without knowing what place you will occupy in it.
contenu_vulgarise:
Imagine a room where the rules that will organize all of society are being negotiated: taxes, schools, health, inheritance. Around the table, everyone defends his own interests: the rich man wants low taxes, the poor man broad redistribution, the healthy man low health-insurance contributions. No stable agreement would come out of it, because everyone already knows what place he occupies and negotiates to keep it.

In 1971, in *A Theory of Justice*, the American philosopher John Rawls proposes a thought experiment to get out of this impasse: what if no one at the table knew what place he would occupy once the rules were set?

## The Original Position

Rawls calls this device the original position, and its central element is the veil of ignorance. Behind this veil, the negotiators know nothing of what would set them apart in real life: their sex, their social origin, their health, their talents, and even their religious or political convictions. They do know general things about human societies: that scarce resources exist, that there are different conceptions of the good life, the basic principles of economics.

Under these conditions, what rules would they choose? Rawls answers: prudent rules, which protect the position of the worst-off, because, behind the veil, each negotiator could very well be that person once the veil is lifted. He calls this reasoning the maximin principle: one chooses the option whose worst case is the least bad, rather than the one that maximizes an average gain one might just as well never collect.

## What This Shifts

The tool does not serve only to ground a theory of social justice; it quietly turns around any debate about a rule. A company writing its internal regulations, a collective dividing up tasks, parents setting rules for several children: the question “would I accept this rule if I did not know what role I would hold in it?” immediately shifts particular interest toward something else.

It does not settle everything. Rawls himself specifies that his negotiators are neither gamblers nor daredevils: parties who loved risk would probably choose different rules behind the same veil. The device therefore does not eliminate the debate about what justice demands: it only shifts the point from which one discusses it, from a table where everyone knows his place to a table where no one yet knows it.

carte.punch: To judge a rule just, imagine it without knowing what place you will hold in it.
carte.idee: In 1971, Rawls imagines negotiators who know nothing of their own place in the society to come: sex, wealth, talents. Behind this veil of ignorance, they would choose rules that protect the worst-off, because they could be him.

quiz.question: Why does Rawls place his negotiators behind a “veil of ignorance”?
choix: So that none of them chooses rules according to the place he will occupy
To keep them from knowing the laws already in force in their country
To guarantee that the negotiation remains strictly anonymous and confidential
To force them to adopt the same rules as the previous generation
quiz.explication: If they knew their own future place (rich or poor, healthy or not), the negotiators would defend that position rather than just rules in general. Not knowing one's own place forces one to choose rules one would accept whatever role one ends up holding, which has nothing to do with the anonymity of the discussion or the renewal of an already established order.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the principle Rawls calls maximin designate?
choix: Choosing the option that maximizes the average gain of all the negotiators
Choosing the most popular option among all the negotiators present
Choosing the option whose worst case is the least bad for oneself
Choosing the option that was adopted by the previous generation
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Rawls calls maximin the reasoning that consists of choosing the option whose worst case is the least bad, rather than the one that maximizes an uncertain average gain.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the negotiators still know, behind the veil of ignorance, according to the text?
choix: The exact amount of their future personal fortune
Their own talents and their religious convictions
The social place they will occupy once the veil is lifted
General things about human societies, such as the scarcity of resources
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The negotiators do not know their own place, but they do know general things about human societies: scarce resources, different conceptions of the good life, economic principles.
